title: Growth monitoring, centile charts and faltering growth
blurb: Interpret early weight loss and centile charts using NICE NG75, recognise faltering growth and plan measurement, feeding support and monitoring.
question: A 9-month-old whose birthweight was on the 50th centile now weighs just below the 9th centile. The parents ask whether this matters. How should the nurse interpret the chart and what happens next?

teach.body: Faltering growth is a slower rate of weight gain in infancy or childhood than expected for the child's age and sex, judged by a fall across centile lines on a growth chart. Plain English: the child's weight is drifting down the chart away from where they started. It is a sign to assess, not a diagnosis, and often has no single cause.

teach.caption: If more than 10% is lost, weigh again at intervals depending on concern, but no more often than daily.

teach.caption: A centile space is the gap between two adjacent centile lines on the UK-WHO growth charts.

items: Measure LENGTH from birth to 2 years; measure HEIGHT over 2 years.
Plot this and previous measurements on the UK-WHO growth charts to see the trend over time.
Over 2 years, work out the BMI centile: below the 2nd may be undernutrition or small build; below the 0.4th suggests probable undernutrition.
Record all measurements in the parent-held Personal Child Health Record (red book).

steps.label: Detailed feeding history
steps.sub: Consider observing a feed or meal

steps.label: Further tests
steps.sub: Only if the assessment points to them

teach.caption: In a child who appears well, extra investigations rarely find an underlying disorder (NG75 1.2.13).

teach.h: Support breastfeeding if formula is added
teach.body: Supplementing a breastfed baby with formula may increase weight gain but often ends breastfeeding. If supplementation is used, support the mother to keep breastfeeding, advise expressing to protect supply, and give any available breast milk before formula.

teach.caption: Weighing more often than needed can add to parental anxiety (NG75 1.2.28).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Poppy at the health visiting clinic
items: Poppy, 10 months, had a birthweight on the 50th centile; she now weighs just below the 9th centile, a fall across 2 centile spaces.
Nurse Kemi recognises this meets the NG75 threshold for a baby born between the 9th and 91st centiles.
She takes a feeding history, checks development and family circumstances, and arranges assessment including consideration of UTI and coeliac disease.
Together with the parents she agrees goals: relaxed family mealtimes, no coercive feeding, 3 meals and 2 snacks, fortnightly weighing, and a review date.

teach.text: Measure LENGTH lying down under 2 years and HEIGHT standing over 2. And remember: the same fall in centile spaces means different things depending on birthweight centile (1, 2 or 3 spaces).

items: Early loss over 10% of birth weight, or not back to birth weight by 3 weeks: assess and support feeding.
Concern: fall of 1+ spaces (birthweight under 9th), 2+ (9th-91st), 3+ (over 91st), or weight below 2nd centile.
Length to 2 years, height after; plot on UK-WHO charts; record in the red book.
Assess feeding, development and social context; consider UTI and coeliac; limit other tests.
Management plan with parents; responsive, non-coercive feeding; tube feeding is a last resort.

summary: You can now interpret early weight loss and centile changes against NICE NG75 thresholds, measure and plot growth correctly, and plan assessment, feeding support and monitoring with parents. You can also explain why weighing too often and unnecessary tests are avoided.

A.q: Amara, a breastfed baby, weighed 3.5 kg at birth. On day 4 she weighs 3.1 kg. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Expected loss: recheck at the 6-8 week review
Loss of more than 10%: assess and support feeding
Loss under 5%: no action is needed
Loss of more than 10%: start formula top-ups now
A.why: 3.5 kg to 3.1 kg is a loss of about 11%. NG75 advises clinical assessment, a feeding history and feeding support when loss exceeds 10%.

whyNot.0: Loss over 10% needs assessment now, not at 6-8 weeks.
whyNot.2: The loss is about 11%, not under 5%.
whyNot.3: Formula is not the automatic first step; assessment and breastfeeding support come first, and supplementation often ends breastfeeding.

A.q: By what age have most babies returned to their birth weight, according to NICE NG75?
options: 10 days
2 weeks
6 weeks
3 weeks
A.why: NG75 1.1.1: most infants have returned to their birth weight by 3 weeks of age.

whyNot.0: Many babies regain birth weight earlier, but NG75 uses 3 weeks as the marker.
whyNot.1: 2 weeks is a common teaching figure, but NG75 states 3 weeks.
whyNot.2: 6 weeks is well beyond the NG75 marker of 3 weeks.

A.q: Finley, 18 months, is seen in clinic with faltering growth. How should his linear growth be measured?
options: Length, lying down
Standing height
Mid-upper arm circumference
Head circumference
A.why: NG75 1.2.2: measure length from birth to 2 years old and height over 2 years.

whyNot.1: Standing height is used over 2 years of age.
whyNot.2: Arm circumference is not the NG75 measure of linear growth.
whyNot.3: Head circumference is measured for other reasons, not linear growth.

B.q: Ivy, 7 months, had a birthweight on the 98th centile. Her weight is now on the 75th centile, a fall across 2 centile spaces. What does NG75 suggest?
options: This meets the threshold for faltering growth
This alone does not reach the NG75 threshold
She needs an urgent tube feeding assessment
This is concerning as she is below the 91st
B.why: For a birthweight above the 91st centile, NG75 sets the threshold at a fall across 3 or more centile spaces. A 2-space fall does not reach it, though the trend should be monitored.

whyNot.0: A 2-space fall is the threshold for birthweights between the 9th and 91st centiles, not above the 91st.
whyNot.2: Tube feeding is a last resort after specialist assessment and other interventions.
whyNot.3: Falling below the 91st centile is not itself a threshold.

B.q: Harvey, 4 months, is being monitored at home for faltering growth. His mother wants him weighed every 2 days. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Weigh him daily to catch any change early
Weigh him every 2 days as she prefers
Weigh him monthly until he is 1 year old
Weigh him usually no more than weekly
B.why: NG75 1.2.27: between 1 and 6 months, usually weigh no more often than weekly; more frequent weighing can increase anxiety.

whyNot.0: Daily weighing is the maximum for babies under 1 month.
whyNot.1: Weighing every 2 days is more often than recommended at 4 months.
whyNot.2: Monthly weighing applies from 1 year of age.

B.q: Leo, 14 months, has faltering growth. He is well and his feeding history shows long, stressful mealtimes where his parents push him to finish. Which advice fits NG75?
options: Offer high-calorie milk drinks between meals
Keep him at the table until he finishes
Relaxed family meals and avoid coercive feeding
Arrange blood tests to look for a cause
B.why: NG75 1.2.19 recommends relaxed, enjoyable mealtimes, eating together, letting young children feed themselves and be messy, and avoiding coercive feeding.

whyNot.0: Too many energy-dense drinks, including milk, can reduce appetite for food (NG75 1.2.22).
whyNot.1: Coercive and punitive feeding should be avoided.
whyNot.3: In a well child, further investigations rarely find a cause; tests should follow clinical indication.

C.q: Jasmine, 7 weeks, is breastfed and has faltering growth. The team recommends supplementing with formula. What should the nurse advise her mother?
options: Give formula first, then breastfeed if she is hungry
Stop breastfeeding to measure intake accurately
Swap to formula until weight is back on track
Keep breastfeeding, express, and give breast milk first
C.why: NG75 1.2.18: support continued breastfeeding, advise expressing to protect supply, and give any available breast milk before formula.

whyNot.0: Breast milk should be given before formula.
whyNot.1: Stopping breastfeeding is not recommended; supplementation often ends it already.
whyNot.2: Replacing breastfeeding with formula loses the benefits and is not advised.

C.q: Sam, 6, is reviewed for poor growth. His BMI is plotted and lies below the 0.4th centile. What does this suggest?
options: Probable undernutrition needing assessment
A small build that needs no action
Normal variation for his age
A primary growth disorder
C.why: NG75 1.2.4: a BMI below the 0.4th centile suggests probable undernutrition that needs assessment and intervention.

whyNot.1: Below the 2nd centile may reflect small build; below the 0.4th suggests probable undernutrition.
whyNot.2: A BMI below the 0.4th centile is not normal variation.
whyNot.3: A primary growth disorder is suggested when height is well below the mid-parental centile, not by a low BMI.

C.q: Ruby, 11 months, has faltering growth. Her mother has postnatal depression and the family has recently moved into temporary housing. What does NG75 advise about these factors?
options: They exclude a medical cause for faltering growth
They are associated factors to include in assessment
They mean a safeguarding referral is required now
They are unrelated and should be managed elsewhere
C.why: NG75 asks for clinical, developmental and social assessment and notes maternal postnatal depression or anxiety is associated with faltering growth; several factors may contribute.

whyNot.0: Social factors do not exclude medical causes; a full assessment is still needed.
whyNot.2: Faltering growth is not automatically a safeguarding issue; NG75 asks to consider features that raise safeguarding concerns.
whyNot.3: These factors are part of the assessment, not separate from it.

reteach.title: Read the chart like a road
reteach.question: If a child starts in one lane of the growth chart, why does it matter when they drift across lanes?

blocks.body: Healthy children usually stay roughly in their own 'lane' between centile lines. Drifting downwards across lanes means weight gain has slowed. The bigger the baby started, the more lanes they can drift before it matters, because larger babies often settle lower.

blocks.text: Whatever the birthweight, a current weight below the 2nd centile is a concern.

explain.body: Some loss in the first days is normal and usually stops by day 3-4. Loss over 10%, or not back to birth weight by 3 weeks, needs assessment and feeding support. Weigh no more often than daily.

test.q: A baby has not regained birth weight by 3 weeks. What should happen?
options: Clinical assessment and feeding support
Reassurance until the 6-8 week review
Daily weighing for a further month
An immediate switch to formula feeding
test.why: NG75 1.1.3-1.1.4: assess and give feeding support; if not back to birth weight by 3 weeks, consider referral to paediatric services or plan when to reassess.

whyNot.2: Daily weighing for a month is excessive and adds anxiety.
whyNot.3: Feeding assessment and support come before changing feeding method.

explain.body: Concern if weight falls across 1 or more centile spaces (birthweight under the 9th), 2 or more (9th-91st), 3 or more (over 91st), or if current weight is below the 2nd centile.

test.q: A baby's birthweight was on the 5th centile. Which change first meets the NG75 threshold for concern?
options: A fall across 3 centile spaces
A fall across 2 centile spaces
A fall across 1 centile space
A fall below the 0.4th BMI centile
test.why: For birthweight below the 9th centile, a fall across 1 or more centile spaces is the threshold.

whyNot.0: 3 spaces is the threshold for birthweight above the 91st.
whyNot.1: 2 spaces is the threshold for birthweight between the 9th and 91st.
whyNot.3: BMI centiles are used over 2 years, not for infant weight thresholds.

explain.body: Length to 2 years, height after 2. Plot on UK-WHO charts with previous measurements. Over 2, use BMI centiles. Record in the red book.

test.q: Where should growth measurements for a child with faltering growth be recorded?
options: The nursery key worker file
The ward observation chart
The hospital discharge letter
The parent-held red book
test.why: NG75 1.2.5: record all growth measurements in the parent- or carer-held Personal Child Health Record.

whyNot.0: Nursery records are not health records; NG75 specifies the parent-held record.
whyNot.1: Observation charts are for vital signs, not long-term growth.
whyNot.2: Discharge letters summarise care but are not the growth record.

explain.body: Agree a plan with goals and monitoring. Advise relaxed family meals, self-feeding, regular meals and snacks, no coercion, and not too many milky drinks. Consider dietitian referral and supplements if needed. Tube feeding only after specialist assessment and when other measures have failed.

test.q: When does NG75 suggest considering enteral tube feeding for faltering growth?
options: As soon as weight falls 2 centile spaces
After specialist assessment and other measures fail
When parents find mealtimes stressful
When the child refuses an oral supplement
test.why: NG75 1.2.25: consider tube feeding only with serious concern, completed specialist MDT assessment, and failure of other interventions.

whyNot.0: A 2-space fall triggers assessment, not tube feeding.
whyNot.2: Stressful mealtimes call for feeding advice and support.
whyNot.3: Refusing one supplement does not on its own meet the criteria.
